interactions.label: Which of the following clinical findings in a young woman with hirsutism should

params.question: Which of the following clinical findings in a young woman with hirsutism should raise suspicion for an androgen-secreting tumour rather than PCOS?

answers.text: Oligomenorrhoea with cycles every six weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oligomenorrhoea — cycles occurring fewer than eight times a year — is the most common menstrual pattern in PCOS. It is a hallmark of typical PCOS, not a sign of an androgen-secreting tumour.

answers.text: Rapidly progressive hirsutism with voice deepening

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Virilisation signs — rapid-onset hirsutism, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly — point to markedly elevated androgens from an ovarian or adrenal tumour, warranting urgent investigation.

answers.text: Acne along the jawline

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Jawline acne is a common androgenic feature in PCOS, driven by mildly elevated androgens. It does not suggest a more sinister androgen source.

answers.text: Acanthosis nigricans in the axillae

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acanthosis nigricans signals underlying insulin resistance, a metabolic feature commonly seen in PCOS. It does not raise suspicion for a tumour.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key red flags for an androgen-secreting tumour are rapid progression over months (not years) and virilisation signs: voice deepening and clitoromegaly. These distinguish it from the gradual, mild hyperandrogenism of PCOS.
Correct. Virilisation — rapid-onset hirsutism, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly — signals markedly elevated androgens and warrants urgent imaging to exclude an androgen-secreting tumour.

interactions.label: In the pathophysiology of PCOS, hyperinsulinaemia drives ovarian androgen excess

params.question: In the pathophysiology of PCOS, hyperinsulinaemia drives ovarian androgen excess primarily by:

answers.text: Stimulating aromatase activity in granulosa cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aromatase in granulosa cells converts androgens to oestrogens. While this contributes to oestrone excess in PCOS, it actually consumes androgens rather than driving their production.

answers.text: Enhancing CYP17A1 activity in ovarian theca cells along with LH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Insulin acts synergistically with LH on ovarian theca cells to upregulate CYP17A1, the key enzyme driving androgen synthesis. Simultaneously, insulin suppresses hepatic SHBG, increasing free circulating androgen levels.

answers.text: Increasing sex hormone-binding globulin production by the liver

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Insulin actually suppresses hepatic SHBG production. Lower SHBG means more free androgen circulates in the blood, worsening the clinical picture — the opposite of what this option states.

answers.text: Promoting selection of a dominant ovarian follicle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The opposite occurs in PCOS. Excess androgen blocks normal follicular maturation, causing multiple small follicles to stall rather than allowing a single dominant follicle to emerge — producing the characteristic polycystic appearance on ultrasound.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the mechanism: insulin acts on theca cells (not granulosa cells) to boost CYP17A1 alongside LH, increasing androgen synthesis. It also suppresses SHBG, allowing more free androgen to circulate.

Correct. Hyperinsulinaemia and LH together upregulate CYP17A1 in theca cells, driving androgen overproduction. Insulin also suppresses SHBG, amplifying free androgen levels and completing the vicious cycle.

interactions.label: A 25-year-old woman has oligomenorrhoea and a raised serum testosterone, but her

params.question: A 25-year-old woman has oligomenorrhoea and a raised serum testosterone, but her transvaginal ultrasound shows normal ovarian morphology. TSH, prolactin, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are all within normal limits. What is the most appropriate conclusion?

answers.text: She does not have PCOS because polycystic ovaries are absent on ultrasound

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Polycystic ovarian morphology is only one of the three Rotterdam features. A woman with oligo-anovulation and hyperandrogenism fulfils two of three criteria and can be diagnosed with PCOS even with normal-appearing ovaries.

answers.text: She meets the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS, as two of three features are present and mimics have been excluded

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Rotterdam criteria require any two of three features. With oligo-anovulation and biochemical hyperandrogenism present, and common mimics (thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, late-onset CAH) excluded, the diagnosis of PCOS is confirmed.

answers.text: She needs an ACTH stimulation test before any diagnosis can be made

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An ACTH stimulation test confirms late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia when morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone is elevated. Here, 17-OHP is already normal, making CAH very unlikely — further testing is not required.

answers.text: She should be diagnosed with hyperandrogenism of unknown cause rather than PCOS

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When a woman meets two of three Rotterdam criteria and common mimics have been excluded by appropriate investigations, the correct diagnosis is PCOS. There is no need for an indeterminate label.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: PCOS is diagnosed when any two of the three Rotterdam features are present AND mimics have been excluded. No single feature, including polycystic morphology, is required on its own.

Correct. PCOS requires any two of three Rotterdam features plus exclusion of mimics. Polycystic morphology is not mandatory — oligomenorrhoea plus hyperandrogenism is sufficient when other causes have been ruled out.

interactions.label: Which investigation most reliably distinguishes late-onset congenital adrenal hy

params.question: Which investigation most reliably distinguishes late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia from PCOS in a woman presenting with hirsutism and oligomenorrhoea?

answers.text: Serum prolactin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serum prolactin screens for hyperprolactinaemia, which suppresses GnRH pulsatility and causes menstrual irregularity. It does not help distinguish congenital adrenal hyperplasia from PCOS.

answers.text: 24-hour urinary free cortisol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This test screens for Cushing syndrome by detecting excess cortisol production. It is not useful for diagnosing congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which involves a defect in cortisol synthesis rather than excess.

answers.text: Morning serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone above 2 ng/mL suggests 21-hydroxylase deficiency, the enzyme defect underlying late-onset CAH. This is the most important genetic mimic of PCOS, found in 4–8% of women with hyperandrogenism.

answers.text: Transvaginal ultrasound of the ovaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Polycystic ovarian morphology can appear in both PCOS and late-onset CAH, making ultrasound unreliable for distinguishing between them. A biochemical marker is needed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Late-onset CAH is caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which leads to accumulation of 17-hydroxyprogesterone. A morning level above 2 ng/mL is the key screening test, confirmed with an ACTH stimulation test.

Correct. Morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the screening test for late-onset CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency — the single most important genetic mimic of PCOS, confirmed by an ACTH stimulation test.

interactions.label: Why are women with PCOS at increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia?

params.question: Why are women with PCOS at increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia?

answers.text: Elevated androgens directly stimulate endometrial proliferation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Androgens are peripherally converted to oestrone by aromatase in adipose tissue. It is this oestrogen, not androgens themselves, that drives endometrial proliferation.

answers.text: Chronic anovulation leads to prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure without progesterone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Without ovulation, no corpus luteum forms, so progesterone is never secreted to oppose oestrogen's proliferative effect on the endometrium. This sustained, unopposed oestrogen exposure raises the risk of hyperplasia and, over time, carcinoma.

answers.text: Insulin resistance causes direct endometrial thickening independent of hormonal changes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While insulin resistance contributes to the metabolic profile of PCOS, endometrial hyperplasia is driven by the hormonal imbalance — specifically, unopposed oestrogen due to chronic anovulation — not by insulin acting directly on the endometrium.

answers.text: Polycystic ovaries secrete excess progesterone that overstimulates the endometrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In PCOS, the problem is a deficiency of progesterone due to anovulation, not an excess. Without progesterone to counterbalance oestrogen, the endometrium proliferates unchecked.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key mechanism is anovulation → no corpus luteum → no progesterone → unopposed oestrogen exposure. This prolonged oestrogen stimulation of the endometrium is what increases the risk of hyperplasia.

Correct. Chronic anovulation means no corpus luteum and no progesterone. The resulting unopposed oestrogen continuously stimulates the endometrium, raising the long-term risk of hyperplasia and carcinoma.
